intro: Devon stares at a two-page article about honeybees and wants to give up. Twenty minutes later he can say the whole thing in two sentences, and he did not copy one word. Priya reads two articles about the same tornado and sees that one is built like a clock and the other like a chain of arrows. A class opens a dusty yearbook and learns something true about their own school that nobody in the building knew.

This unit is about reading to learn: articles, science pages, history pages, charts, maps and websites. You will find the main idea and the details that hold it up. You will spot the five shapes a text can take and take notes that match. You will read a chart like a paragraph, tell a fact from an opinion, and tell a primary source from a secondary one.

By the end, you will be able to take a real question nobody can answer, find good sources, take honest notes, and write an answer with evidence. That is what scientists, reporters and historians do every day. It starts with one sentence in an article that all the others hold up.
bigQuestion: How do you read a text you did not choose and come away knowing something true?

timeline.t: Skim the title, headings and pictures and ask what you want to find out.
Read a paragraph and find the sentence the others hold up: the main idea.
Sort the details that support the idea from the sentences that are just extra.
Read the captions, diagrams, maps and sidebars as part of the text.
Spot the shape: sequence, description, compare, cause and effect, or problem and solution.
Take notes in the shape of the text: a list, two columns, or boxes with arrows.
Read a second text on the same topic and compare what each one keeps and leaves out.
Ask a research question that is specific and that nobody in the room can answer yet.
Find primary and secondary sources, judge which are reliable, and note where each fact came from.
Write the answer in your own words, back it with evidence, and say what is still unknown.

words.d: the most important point a text makes about its topic
a fact, example or reason that supports the main idea
a short retelling of the main idea and biggest details in your own words
to figure out something the text does not say, using clues
the words under or beside a picture that explain it
the way a text is built: sequence, description, compare and contrast, cause and effect, or problem and solution
a word that hints at a text's shape, like first, both, because or solved
something made at the time of an event by a person who was there
something made later by a person who studied the event
what a person thinks or feels; it cannot be proved true or false
using someone else's words or ideas as if they were your own

test.q: "Honeybees" is a topic. Which of these is a main idea?
choices: A honeybee hive works like a busy city
test.why: A main idea is a whole sentence that makes a point about the topic.

test.q: What do supporting details do for a main idea?
choices: Hold it up like table legs
test.why: Details are facts, examples and reasons that prove the main idea.

test.q: Which is a real summary of a paragraph?
choices: The main idea and biggest details in your own words
test.why: A summary is short and in your own words.

test.q: "Maya grabbed her umbrella and boots." The rain is...
test.why: The text never says rain, but the clues point to it.

test.q: Where is a key term's meaning often found on a page?
test.why: Writers bold a key term and often define it in the same sentence.

test.q: You need one date from a long article. Which way of reading is fastest?
test.why: Scanning hunts for one specific thing like a number.

test.q: "First the sky turned green. Next the sirens sounded. Then the funnel touched down." What shape is this?
test.why: First, next, then: events in time order.

test.q: "Warm air rose, so the storm began to spin." Which is the effect?
test.why: The spinning is the result of the rising air.

test.q: Which note shape fits a compare-and-contrast text?
test.why: Two columns put two things side by side.

test.q: The sirens sounded and then the funnel touched down. Did the sirens cause the funnel?
choices: No, close in time is not cause
test.why: Two events close together are not always cause and effect.

test.q: Which is a primary source about a school's opening day in 1959?
choices: A letter written that day by a student
test.why: The letter was made at the time by someone who was there.

test.q: "The playground has three slides." Fact or opinion?
choices: Opinion, because it is about a playground
Fact, because you can count the slides
test.why: It can be checked by counting, so it is a fact.

test.q: Which research question is the right size?
choices: What is everything about the ocean?
Why did our town build a wall of rocks along the lake?
test.why: It is specific, sources can answer it, and you cannot just look.

test.q: You want to keep a source's exact words in your notes. What do you do?
choices: Put quotation marks around them and note the source
Write them in a different color
test.why: Quotation marks are a promise that the words are not yours.

test.q: Which website is most reliable for a school-history question?
choices: One with no author and flashing ads
One about a different school in another state
One that says it is the best site ever
The town's official site with a date and a contact
test.why: You can tell who made it and when, and you can check it.

write.prompt: Pick one of the two tornado articles from Chapter 15. Claim which one would help a new student understand tornadoes better. Use evidence about how each article is built, and explain your reasoning.
tips: Claim: name the article and say it is the better one for a new student.
Evidence: describe its shape (sequence or cause and effect) and one thing it includes that the other leaves out.
Reasoning: explain why that shape and those facts help someone who knows nothing about tornadoes.
The other side: say one thing the other article does well, then explain why your choice still wins.
